To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) the thermal instability can be suppressed by convection, and (2) the thermal instability is a necessary but not sufficient condition for the formation of a gas-pressure-dominated disk.
the standard equilibrium for radiation-supported disks can collapse to a gas-pressure-supported configuration, and that this collapse is driven by convection.

the standard radiation-dominated accretions disks are thermally and convectively stable, and that convective motions lead to a new equilibrium that is thinner than, and more stable than, the standard equilibrium.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following three issues.
the development of a self-regulated, radiation-supported, and gas-pressure-dominated equilibrium in accretion disks.
the development and evolution of convection in radiation-dominated accretions disks, and we find that convection can alter the equilibrium structure of such disks.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
convection is the dominant physical process in radiation-dominated disks.
the radiation pressure-dominated equilibrium is unstable to convective motions and that the end state is either a gas pressure-dominated disk or a thermal instability.
radiation-dominated disks are thermally stable, but only when the dissipation rate is dominated by convection, which is a plausible assumption in the presence of magnetic fields.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the vertical column of a disk is subject to a thermal instability if the vertically integrated dissipated power is independent of the column density, whereas it is subject to a convective instability if the vertically averaged dissipated power is proportional to the column density.
radiation-dominated accretions disks can exist as thin gas-pressure-supported disks, but only if the disk is convectively unstable.
the standard equilibrium for radiation-supported disks is unstable, and that convection plays a critical role in determining the final state of the disk.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the vertical structure of radiation-dominated accretions disks is determined by the balance between the dissipation of gravitational potential energy and the release of internal energy.
the vertical structure of radiation-dominated accretions disks depends strongly on the details of their dissipation mechanisms.
radiation-dominated accretions disks, when subject to convective motions, can settle into a new equilibrium that is thinner, denser, and more luminous than the standard equilibrium.
